grammars.text:
# ─── Whitespace / comments ───────────────────────────────────
ws       = /[ \t]+/
nl       = "\n"
wsNl     = /\s+/
comment  = /#[^\n]*/

# Inter-statement trivia: whitespace, newlines, and comment lines.
# `Options` produces no wrapper node — only `wsNl` or `comment` shows up.
triviaUnit = wsNl | comment
trivias    = (triviaUnit)+

# ─── Leaves ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
identifier = /[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*/
# `=` is included so bare `key=value` after a command name tokenizes as
# a single positional bareword. Real bash doesn't treat `=` as a token
# boundary in arg position — `echo key=val` is one positional. The
# `namedArg` rule below requires a leading `--` or `-`, so unprefixed
# `key=val` falls through to `word` (which uses this bareword).
# A bareword admits regex anchors (`^`, `$`) so patterns like `^[0-9]+$`
# parse as a single token in `[[ … =~ … ]]` and `case` clauses. `$` is
# in the alternation rather than the character class so it can carry a
# negative lookahead: `$` followed by an expansion starter (`{(letter
# digit ? @ * #`) belongs to `expansion` / `varRef`, not the bareword.
# Same trick the `dqLiteral` rule uses inside double-quoted strings.
# `\{\}` is matched as a literal bareword chunk so empty braces parse
# as ordinary text — matches bash, where `{}` (empty) and `{x}` (single
# item) are both literal. The canonical idiom this enables is
# `xargs -I {} sh -c '...'`; without it the LLM gets a parse error on
# something every Unix-trained model writes by reflex. Placed first in
# the alternation so the longer literal wins before the class consumes
# `{` (it doesn't anyway — `{`/`}` aren't in the class — but the
# explicit ordering matches the rest of the grammar's longest-first
# convention).
# The extglob operator chars `? * + @ !` are pulled out of the main class
# into a guarded alternative `[?*+@!](?!\()` so a bareword never swallows
# the operator of a following extglob group (`@(a|b)`): when one of them
# is immediately followed by `(`, the bareword stops and `extglobGroup`
# (a separate wordPart) takes over. Standalone (`a*b`, `x?`, `!`, `a+`)
# they're consumed exactly as before.
# The comma `,` is an ORDINARY word character in bash everywhere except
# brace expansion (`{a,b}`) and arithmetic (`$((a,b))`), both of which are
# separate sub-grammars. So `--ref t8,t9` is one word. The brace-context
# bareword (`braceBareword`, below) deliberately OMITS the comma so the
# comma keeps splitting `braceItem`s inside `{ }`.
bareword   = /(?:\{\}|\\.|\$(?![{(A-Za-z_0-9?@*#])|[?*+@!](?!\()|[a-zA-Z0-9_.\/%:=^~,\[\]-])+/
sqString   = /'(?:\\[\s\S]|[^'\\])*'/

# ─── Expansions ($VAR / ${VAR} / $(...) / $?) ───────────────
# Listed longest-first so the matcher commits to the longer
# prefix (e.g. `${` and `$(` before `$`). `specialVar` covers
# bash's special parameters — currently `$?` only, easy to extend.
# `arithExpansion` matches `$((expr))`, listed before `cmdSub` so its
# `$((` prefix wins first-match over `$(` — and the `~/` COMMITS there:
# once `$((` is seen this IS arithmetic, and a failure inside it is a
# syntax error, never re-read as a cmdSub. That matches bash/POSIX
# (`$((echo hi))` errors; a subshell inside cmdSub is written `$( (…) )`
# with the space) and kills the exponential cross-backtrack: without the
# cut, an input like `$((((((…` was re-parsed as arithmetic at EVERY
# nesting depth of the cmdSub fallback — a 156-byte command was a fatal
# heap OOM (docs/cpu-runaway-audit.md K1).
#
# `bracedVar` uses Block delimiters so the matching `}` is found
# by depth-counted scan BEFORE content parses — nested forms like
# `${var:-${other}}` Just Work because the outer `}` is paired
# with the outer `${` before the inner contents are touched.
# Inside, `bracedBody` dispatches structurally on the form: plain
# identifier (`${VAR}`), or one of the parameter-expansion shapes.
varRef         = "$" + identifier
bracedVar      = ["${"] bracedBody ["}"]
cmdSub         = "$(" + script + ")"
arithExpansion = "$((" ~/ ws? + arithExpr + ws? + "))"
specialVarName = /[?@*#0-9]/
specialVar     = "$" + specialVarName
# Backticks: legacy command substitution equivalent to `$(cmd)`. Same
# trim-trailing-newlines semantics; visitor delegates to _evalCmdSub.
backtickSub    = "`" + script + "`"
expansion      = arithExpansion | bracedVar | cmdSub | backtickSub | specialVar | varRef

# Process substitution: `<(cmd)` exposes cmd's OUTPUT as a readable file
# path; `>(cmd)` exposes a writable file path whose contents are fed to
# cmd's stdin after the outer command runs. The visitor runs the inner
# script against a temp path in the FileStore and substitutes that path as
# the word. Mirrors `cmdSub`'s `"$(" + script + ")"` shape. These are
# wordParts (tried before the `<`/`>` redirect operators can claim the
# leading char, since a redirect's `< word` can't start a word with `(`).
procSubIn      = "<(" + script + ")"
procSubOut     = ">(" + script + ")"

# ─── Parameter expansion (`${var…}`) — body shapes ──────────
# bracedBody dispatches on which form is inside the braces. The
# visitor reads the matched alternative's name (cpat Options
# collapses to the matched alternative — there's no `bracedBody`
# wrapper node, so the body child carries one of: `pexDefault`,
# `pexLength`, `pexSubstr`, `pexStrip`, `pexReplace`, `pexCase`,
# `pexIndirect`, `identifier`, …). Order matters: longest/most-specific
# first so a `${var:-d}` doesn't bind as a bare identifier before the
# operator is even examined, and `pexDefault` stays ahead of `pexSubstr`
# so `${var:-d}` parses as default (op `:-`) rather than substring (op
# `:` + arg `-d`). `pexIndirect` is leading-`!`-keyed and `pexLength`
# is leading-`#`-keyed — both are disjoint from the identifier-first
# rules and from each other. The remaining pex* rules (`pexStrip`,
# `pexReplace`, `pexCase`) have disjoint operator sets too, so their
# relative ordering is purely stylistic.
# `pexPositionalSlice` and `pexSpecialLength` come before the identifier-keyed
# rules because their leading char (`@`/`*`/`#`) can never start an identifier;
# `pexSpecial` is LAST of the three so the longer forms commit first
# (`${@:2}` must not bind as a bare `${@}` with a stray `:2`).
bracedBody = pexSpecialLength | pexPositionalSlice
           | pexLength | pexArrayIndices | pexIndirect
           | pexDefault | pexSubstr | pexStrip | pexReplace | pexCase
           | pexTransform | pexArrayRead | pexSpecial | identifier

# ─── Braced special parameters — `${@}`, `${*}`, `${#}`, `${1}` ───
# The unbraced forms (`$@`, `$#`, `$1`) are matched by `specialVar` in the
# expansion rule. Inside braces NOTHING accepted them: every `bracedBody`
# alternative was keyed on `identifier`, which is `[A-Za-z_]…`, so `"${@}"`
# was a hard parse error that killed the whole script while `"$@"` worked.
# `${10}` and up — the only way to reach a positional past 9 — failed for the
# same reason.
#
# The name set matches `specialVarName` plus multi-digit positionals.
pexSpecialName = /[?@*#$!]|[0-9]+/
pexSpecial     = pexSpecialName

# `${#@}` / `${#*}` — the COUNT of positional parameters, the special-param
# twin of `${#arr[@]}`. Distinct from `${#}` (also the count, but reached
# through `pexSpecial`) and from `${#var}` (string length, `pexLength`).
pexSpecialLength = "#" + /[@*]/

# `${@:offset}` / `${@:offset:length}` — slice the positional parameters.
# `${@:2}` ("everything after the first argument") is the idiom this exists
# for. Reuses `pexNum` so the slots accept the same expansions the string
# substring form does.
pexPositionalSlice = /[@*]/ + ":" + pexNum + pexSubstrLen?

# `${#var}` — character length of `$var`. With an optional `[…]`
# subscript: `${#arr[N]}` is the length of element N's string;
# `${#arr[@]}` and `${#arr[*]}` are the element count of the array.
# The leading `#` is the only parameter-expansion form that starts
# with a non-identifier, so disambiguation is structural — no other
# shape begins with `#`.
pexLength = "#" + identifier + arraySubscript?

# `${arr[N]}` indexed read, `${arr[@]}` / `${arr[*]}` "all elements"
# expansions. The visitor reads the subscript word and dispatches:
# `@`/`*` produce a joined-by-IFS string (documented divergence from
# bash, which preserves element boundaries inside double quotes);
# numeric subscripts read that one element.
pexArrayRead = identifier + arraySubscript

# `${var@op}` — transform operators (bash's `@`-suffix family):
#   @Q  quote the value so it can be re-read as shell input
#   @E  interpret ANSI-C backslash escapes (`\n`, `\t`, `\xNN`, …)
#   @P  prompt-style escape expansion (a near-superset of @E here)
#   @A  print the `declare` statement that would recreate the variable
#   @a  the variable's attribute flags (`a` indexed, `A` associative)
# Optional `[…]` subscript so `${arr[@]@Q}` transforms each element.
# Must precede `pexArrayRead`/`identifier` in `bracedBody` so the
# trailing `@op` isn't left unconsumed.
pexTransformOp = /@[QEPAa]/
pexTransform   = identifier + arraySubscript? + pexTransformOp

# `${!arr[@]}` / `${!arr[*]}` → indices of the array. Distinct from
# `${!var}` (indirect) and `${!prefix*}` (name list) — the bracketed
# form switches to indices semantics. Order in `bracedBody` puts
# `pexArrayIndices` before `pexIndirect` so the bracketed form wins.
pexArrayIndices = "!" + identifier + arraySubscript

# `${var<op>arg}` — default / alt / assign / error family.
# Eight operators total; their semantics split on whether `:`
# treats empty as unset:
#   :-  -   default if unset (or empty, for `:-`)
#   :=  =   assign default + return it (same unset/empty rule)
#   :?  ?   error if unset (or empty, for `:?`)
#   :+  +   alt if SET (and non-empty, for `:+`)
#
# Listed longest-first so the matcher commits to `:-` before `-`
# (the cpat PEG won't backtrack across an Options match).
pexOpDefault  = ":-" | ":=" | ":?" | ":+" | "-" | "=" | "?" | "+"
# Optional `arraySubscript` before the operator lets `${arr[i]:-d}` /
# `${m[key]:-d}` work. The visitor extracts the array element (or
# scalar var when subscript is absent) as the "subject" the op
# operates on. Assigning forms (`:=`/`=`) write back to arr[i]/m[k].
pexDefault    = identifier + arraySubscript? + pexOpDefault + pexArg?

# The argument inside `${var:-ARG}` is one word, but with two
# divergences from a plain shell word:
#   1. Spaces are allowed — `${var:?file not found}` is valid.
#   2. `$`/`${`/`$(` still trigger expansion inside the arg.
# `pexArgLiteral` matches any run of chars that aren't `$`, `{`,
# `}`, or `\` — plus `\X` escapes and bare-`$` that isn't an
# expansion starter (mirrors `bareword`'s negative-lookahead trick).
# Stops cleanly at `}` so the surrounding Block close matches.
pexArgLiteral = /(?:\\[\s\S]|\$(?![{(A-Za-z_0-9?@*#])|[^${}\\])+/
pexArgPart    = expansion | pexArgLiteral
pexArg        = (pexArgPart)+

# `${var:offset}` and `${var:offset:length}` — substring extraction.
# Both slots are evaluated as integers (bash treats them as full
# arithmetic expressions; we accept the same shape but evaluate via
# parseInt — full `$((…))` works because expansions run as a child).
# `pexNumLiteral` is like `pexArgLiteral` but also excludes `:` so
# the second colon separator (length) doesn't get absorbed into the
# offset's literal run. Spaces are still allowed inside slots (for
# `${var: -5}` "from end" idiom — not yet implemented, but the
# grammar shape leaves room for it).
pexNumLiteral = /(?:\\[\s\S]|\$(?![{(A-Za-z_0-9?@*#])|[^${}:\\])+/
pexNumPart    = expansion | pexNumLiteral
pexNum        = (pexNumPart)+
pexSubstrLen  = ":" + pexNum
# Subscript form supported: `${arr[i]:offset:length}`.
pexSubstr     = identifier + arraySubscript? + ":" + pexNum + pexSubstrLen?

# `${var<op>pattern}` — prefix/suffix strip family. Four operators:
#   #   strip shortest matching prefix
#   ##  strip longest matching prefix
#   %   strip shortest matching suffix
#   %%  strip longest matching suffix
# The pattern is evaluated as a normal pex-arg (so `$VAR`, `$(cmd)`,
# and escapes work inside it) and then matched as a bash glob via
# `globMatch`. Operators listed longest-first so `##` commits before
# `#` (cpat PEG, no backtrack across Options). The arg reuses `pexArg`
# rather than introducing a new type — bash treats the strip pattern
# as a word with the same expansion rules as the default-form arg.
pexOpStrip = "##" | "#" | "%%" | "%"
pexStrip   = identifier + arraySubscript? + pexOpStrip + pexArg?

# `${var/pat/repl}` and family — pattern replacement.
#   /     replace first match
#   //    replace all matches
#   /#    replace if matched at start (prefix anchor)
#   /%    replace if matched at end (suffix anchor)
#
# Pattern syntax is bash-glob (matched via `globMatchString` — `*`
# unrestricted across `/`, like the rest of bash's string-matching
# contexts). The pattern is bounded by an unescaped `/` (start of
# replacement) or `}` (end of expansion); `\/` is a literal `/` in
# the pattern. The replacement reuses `pexArg`, so `/` is allowed
# inside it (no escape needed there).
#
# Both pattern and replacement are optional:
#   `${var//}` → empty pattern, empty replacement (no-op, matches bash)
#   `${var/pat}` → omitted replacement is treated as empty
#
# Operators listed longest-first (`//` before `/`, `/#` and `/%`
# before `/`) so cpat commits to the most specific operator first.
pexOpReplace        = "//" | "/#" | "/%" | "/"
pexReplacePatLiteral = /(?:\\[\s\S]|\$(?![{(A-Za-z_0-9?@*#])|[^${}\/\\])+/
pexReplacePatPart    = expansion | pexReplacePatLiteral
pexReplacePat        = (pexReplacePatPart)+
pexReplaceRepl       = "/" + pexArg?
pexReplace           = identifier + arraySubscript? + pexOpReplace + pexReplacePat? + pexReplaceRepl?

# `${var^}` / `${var^^}` / `${var,}` / `${var,,}` — case conversion.
#   ^   uppercase the first character
#   ^^  uppercase every character
#   ,   lowercase the first character
#   ,,  lowercase every character
#
# The optional arg is a single-character bash glob: when present, only
# characters matching it get transformed. `${var^^[aeiou]}` uppercases
# vowels and leaves consonants alone. Without an arg, every character
# in scope is transformed unconditionally. Operators listed longest-
# first so `^^` commits before `^` and `,,` before `,`.
pexOpCase = "^^" | "^" | ",," | ","
pexCase   = identifier + arraySubscript? + pexOpCase + pexArg?

# `${!var}` — indirect lookup (value of the variable named by $var).
# `${!prefix*}` / `${!prefix@}` — names of variables whose names start
# with `prefix`. Both name-list forms emit a string with the first
# `$IFS` character as the separator; word-splitting on the unquoted
# expansion then produces multiple args, which is the most useful
# bash idiom (`for v in ${!FOO*}; do …`). The bash `*`-vs-`@` distinction
# only matters inside double quotes — we treat them identically because
# the shell has no way to emit "N separate words" from a single
# expansion (no array infrastructure yet).
pexOpNameList = "*" | "@"
pexIndirect   = "!" + identifier + pexOpNameList?

# ─── Double-quoted strings (with interpolation) ──────────────
# Inside "...", split into literal runs and expansions.
# A literal run can contain `\X` escapes and bare `$` only when the
# `$` isn't the start of a recognized expansion (negative lookahead).
dqLiteral = /(?:\\[\s\S]|\$(?![{(A-Za-z_?@*#0-9])|[^"\\$`])+/
dqPart    = expansion | dqLiteral
dqParts   = (dqPart)+
dqString  = "\"" + dqParts? + "\""

# ─── Brace expansion ({a,b,c}) ───────────────────────────────
# `{a,b,c}` is one wordPart; the visitor expands a word with brace
# parts via cartesian product before evaluating each alternative.
# Single-item braces (`{only}`) parse but the visitor leaves them
# literal — matching bash, where expansion needs ≥2 items.
#
# A `braceItem` uses `braceWordPart`, whose bareword (`braceBareword`)
# is the comma-FREE variant — identical to the top-level `bareword`
# minus the `,`. This is what lets the comma keep splitting items here
# (`braceMore`) while staying an ordinary character in a plain word.
# Without the split, `{a,b,c}` would collapse to one item and lose the
# structured children the visitor needs to expand `{$x,$y}` per-item.
braceBareword = /(?:\{\}|\\.|\$(?![{(A-Za-z_0-9?@*#])|[?*+@!](?!\()|[a-zA-Z0-9_.\/%:=^~\[\]-])+/
braceWordPart = procSubIn | procSubOut | expansion | braceList | sqString | dqString | extglobGroup | braceBareword
braceItem  = (braceWordPart)+
braceMore  = "," + braceItem
braceMores = (braceMore)+
braceList  = "{" + braceItem + braceMores? + "}"

# ─── Extglob group (shopt extglob) ───────────────────────────
# `?(…)` `*(…)` `+(…)` `@(…)` `!(…)` — one operator char glued to a
# `|`-separated list of sub-patterns, captured as a single wordPart. The
# visitor reads the node's raw text and hands it to the glob matcher
# (`glob.cpat`), which does the actual extglob→regex translation; here we
# only need to delimit the token correctly.
#
# Nesting (`@(a|@(b))`) is handled by ordinary recursion (`extglobItem` →
# `extglobGroup`), NOT a `Block` depth-scan — a raw scan would miscount
# escaped parens. `extglobEsc` is tried before any literal so `\(`/`\)`/
# `\|` are consumed as literals and never shift the group's nesting.
# `extglobOpenAhead` guards a literal run so it stops before a nested
# `op(`; whitespace ends the run (and so the word).
extglobOpenAhead = /[?*+@!]\(/
extglobOp        = /[?*+@!]/
extglobOpen      = "("
extglobClose     = ")"
extglobEsc       = /\\./
extglobInChar    = /[^()|\s\\]/
extglobInUnit    = !extglobOpenAhead + extglobInChar
extglobInRun     = (extglobInUnit)+
extglobItem      = extglobGroup | extglobEsc | extglobInRun
extglobAlt       = (extglobItem)*
extglobAlts      = (extglobAlt, "|")+
extglobGroup     = extglobOp + extglobOpen + extglobAlts + extglobClose

# ─── Word (compound token) ───────────────────────────────────
# A shell word is a glued sequence of bareword/quote/expansion
# parts (no whitespace between them). Most argument positions use this.
# `extglobGroup` precedes `bareword` so an `op(` commits to a group
# before the operator char is read as a bareword.
# `$'…'` — ANSI-C quoting. The body's backslash escapes (`\n`, `\t`, `\xNN`,
# `\uNNNN`, `\0NNN`) are interpreted, unlike a plain `'…'` where every
# character is literal. `ansi_c.ts` has done the interpreting all along, but it
# was only ever wired to `printf` and `${v@E}` — as a WORD, `$'a\tb'` fell
# through to `bareword` `$` plus an ordinary single-quoted string and came out
# as the seven literal characters `$a\tb`. That made `IFS=$'\n'` — much the
# most common use — silently set IFS to a backslash and an `n`.
#
# Listed before `expansion` and `bareword` so the `$'` prefix commits here
# first; `expansion` never claims it (none of its forms accept a quote after
# the `$`), so without this rule the `$` is simply eaten as a bareword.
ansiCString = /\$'(?:\\[\s\S]|[^'\\])*'/

wordPart = procSubIn | procSubOut | ansiCString | expansion | braceList | sqString | dqString | extglobGroup | bareword
word     = (wordPart)+

# Assignment-value word: same idea, but its bareword variant allows
# `=` so values like `FOO=a=b=c` work without quotes.
# `\{\}` allowed as a literal chunk for parity with `bareword` — keeps
# assignment values like `FOO={}` working without quoting.
assignBareword = /(?:\{\}|\\.|[a-zA-Z0-9_.\/@%+:=*?,\[\]~-])+/
assignWordPart = ansiCString | expansion | sqString | dqString | assignBareword
assignWord     = (assignWordPart)+

# ─── Arguments ───────────────────────────────────────────────
# `namedArg` requires a leading `--` or `-` — matches bash. Bare
# `key=value` after a command name is a positional (handled by the
# `word` fall-through and bareword's `=` allowance above). The
# standalone `FOO=bar` statement and the `FOO=bar cmd` prefix form
# are handled by `assignment` / `prefixedCommand` below; those use
# `assignWord` directly, not `namedArg`, so this rule only governs
# what happens to `=` tokens AFTER a command name.
argName       = /(?:--|-)[a-zA-Z_][a-zA-Z0-9_-]*/
argEquals     = "="
namedArg      = argName + argEquals + word
arg           = namedArg | word

# ─── Redirects ───────────────────────────────────────────────
# `<<HEREDOC` is a synthetic operator emitted by the heredoc preprocessing
# pass — the user writes `<< EOF\n...\nEOF` and the preprocessor rewrites
# it to a single-line `<<HEREDOC <string>` form before the grammar runs.
mergeStderrToStdout = "2>&1"
# `>&2` / `1>&2` — send stdout to stderr (mirror of `2>&1`). Ordered in
# the `redirect` options BEFORE `redirectFile` so this commits before
# `writeStdout` (`>`) can match its leading `>` (cpat `|` is ordered
# first-match — the longer/specific form must come first). A single regex
# (not `">&2" | "1>&2"`) so the node keeps the name `dupStdoutToStderr`;
# an Options of inline literals would name the node after the literal.
dupStdoutToStderr   = /1?>&2/
# `>&-` / `1>&-` close stdout, `2>&-` closes stderr (discard the stream).
# Single regex for the stdout form so the node keeps its name; ordered
# before `dupStdoutToStderr`/`writeStdout` so the longer form commits.
closeStdout         = /1?>&-/
closeStderr         = "2>&-"
appendStdout        = ">>"
writeStdout         = ">"
readStdin           = "<"
appendStderr        = "2>>"
writeStderr         = "2>"
heredocOp           = "<<HEREDOC"
heredocBody         = sqString | dqString
heredocRedir        = heredocOp + ws + heredocBody
# `<<<` here-string: feed the literal word + a trailing newline as
# stdin. Common idiom `read x <<< "$y"` parses a string into a var
# without needing a temp file. The grammar puts hereString BEFORE
# heredocRedir / readStdin so the longer `<<<` literal commits first
# (otherwise `<` would match and the rest would fail to parse).
hereStringOp        = "<<<"
hereString          = hereStringOp + ws? + word
# `appendStderr` (`2>>`) before `writeStderr` (`2>`) so the longer op wins.
redirectOpFile      = appendStdout | writeStdout | readStdin | appendStderr | writeStderr
redirectFile        = redirectOpFile + ws? + word
# Close ops (`>&-`/`2>&-`) and dup ops precede `redirectFile` so their
# leading `>`/`2>` doesn't get consumed by `writeStdout`/`writeStderr`.
redirect            = hereString | heredocRedir | mergeStderrToStdout | dupStdoutToStderr
                    | closeStdout | closeStderr | redirectFile

# ─── Command (atom of expr) ─────────────────────────────────
commandName     = word
commandSuffix   = redirect | arg
spacedSuffix    = ws? + commandSuffix
commandSuffixes = (spacedSuffix)+
command         = commandName + commandSuffixes?

# ─── Variable assignment ────────────────────────────────────
# `FOO=bar` standalone is a statement that mutates Shell.vars.
# `FOO=bar cmd args` is a prefix that scopes the assignment to
# that command's frame only. Multiple prefixes are allowed.
assignment      = identifier + argEquals + assignWord
spacedAssign    = assignment + ws
prefixList      = (spacedAssign)+
prefixedCommand = prefixList + command

# ─── Array assignment ───────────────────────────────────────
# `arr=(a b c)` initializes an indexed array (replaces any prior).
# `arr+=(d e)` appends elements. `arr+=value` (no parens) appends
# value to arr[0] for arrays, or concatenates for scalars — but
# we only support the paren form here; scalar string-concat is
# a separate path. Element words go through the same brace/glob
# /IFS-split expansion as command args.
#
# Separators are `wsNl` (whitespace INCLUDING newlines), not plain `ws`:
# bash separates array elements by any whitespace, so the multi-line form
#   arr=(
#     "a"
#     "b"
#   )
# is valid. With newline-less `ws` the rule failed to match the `(`-then-
# newline and the whole `arr=(…)` fell back to a bogus command word.
arrayInitOp     = "+=" | "="
arrayElement    = wsNl? + word
arrayElements   = (arrayElement)+
arrayInit       = identifier + arrayInitOp + "(" + wsNl? + arrayElements? + wsNl? + ")"

# Indexed assignment: `arr[i]=value` (or `arr[i]+=value` for
# append-to-element). The subscript can contain expansions
# (`$VAR`, `${other}`, `$((expr))`) and otherwise any char except
# `]` itself — we can't use the generic `word` because the
# `bareword` regex includes `[` and `]` in its char class, so it
# would greedily eat past the subscript's closing `]`. Same shape
# as `pexArgLiteral` but `]` is also excluded.
arraySubLiteral = /(?:\\[\s\S]|\$(?![{(A-Za-z_0-9?@*#])|[^\]${}"'\\])+/
# arraySubPart admits expansions and quoted strings (so assoc keys
# with spaces / special chars work via `m["hello world"]=x`), plus
# raw literal runs that exclude `]` (subscript terminator) and `"` /
# `'` (handled by the quoted alternatives).
arraySubPart    = expansion | sqString | dqString | arraySubLiteral
arraySubWord    = (arraySubPart)+
# Subscript can be empty (`m[""]` with an empty key, parsed as
# `[" "]` where the dqString is empty). `?` lets the empty-content
# case parse cleanly; the visitor then evaluates to empty text.
arraySubscript  = "[" + arraySubWord? + "]"
arrayIndexedAssign = identifier + arraySubscript + arrayInitOp + assignWord

# ─── Subshell ───────────────────────────────────────────────
# `(cmd1; cmd2)` runs the inner script in an isolated var scope —
# assignments inside don't leak to the outer shell.
subshell = "(" + trivias? + statementList + trivias? + ")"

# ─── Loop keywords (word-bounded) ───────────────────────────
# Each keyword uses a negative-lookahead regex so prefixes like
# `forecast` / `donate` / `breaker` stay as ordinary barewords.
forKw      = /for(?![a-zA-Z0-9_-])/
inKw       = /in(?![a-zA-Z0-9_-])/
doKw       = /do(?![a-zA-Z0-9_-])/
doneKw     = /done(?![a-zA-Z0-9_-])/
breakKw    = /break(?![a-zA-Z0-9_-])/
continueKw = /continue(?![a-zA-Z0-9_-])/
exitKw     = /exit(?![a-zA-Z0-9_-])/
ifKw       = /if(?![a-zA-Z0-9_-])/
thenKw     = /then(?![a-zA-Z0-9_-])/
elifKw     = /elif(?![a-zA-Z0-9_-])/
elseKw     = /else(?![a-zA-Z0-9_-])/
fiKw       = /fi(?![a-zA-Z0-9_-])/
whileKw    = /while(?![a-zA-Z0-9_-])/
untilKw    = /until(?![a-zA-Z0-9_-])/
caseKw     = /case(?![a-zA-Z0-9_-])/
esacKw     = /esac(?![a-zA-Z0-9_-])/
selectKw   = /select(?![a-zA-Z0-9_-])/
functionKw = /function(?![a-zA-Z0-9_-])/
returnKw   = /return(?![a-zA-Z0-9_-])/
localKw    = /local(?![a-zA-Z0-9_-])/
exportKw   = /export(?![a-zA-Z0-9_-])/
shiftKw    = /shift(?![a-zA-Z0-9_-])/
trapKw     = /trap(?![a-zA-Z0-9_-])/
aliasKw    = /alias(?![a-zA-Z0-9_-])/
unaliasKw  = /unalias(?![a-zA-Z0-9_-])/
unsetKw    = /unset(?![a-zA-Z0-9_-])/
evalKw     = /eval(?![a-zA-Z0-9_-])/
letKw      = /let(?![a-zA-Z0-9_-])/
readonlyKw = /readonly(?![a-zA-Z0-9_-])/
typeKw     = /type(?![a-zA-Z0-9_-])/
commandKw  = /command(?![a-zA-Z0-9_-])/
# `source` is the long form. The short form `.` needs a negative
# lookahead that excludes the chars used by file paths (`./foo`,
# `.txt`, `.bashrc`) so the keyword only matches a standalone dot
# followed by whitespace/separator. Word-bounded the same way the
# other keywords are.
sourceLongKw  = /source(?![a-zA-Z0-9_-])/
sourceShortKw = /\.(?![a-zA-Z0-9_.\/])/

# ─── For-loop (list form) ───────────────────────────────────
# `for X in W W W; do BODY; done`. The iteration list reuses
# the standard `word` machinery, so braces and globs expand
# the same way they do for command arguments. The body uses a
# `!doneKw` lookahead at each repeat iteration to keep `done`
# out of the body — otherwise `(statement)+` would greedily
# consume it as a bareword command and the terminator would fail.
loopWord         = ws + word
loopWords        = (loopWord)+
forBodyStatement = !doneKw + statement
forBody          = (forBodyStatement)+
# A bash compound command (including `for ... done`) accepts trailing
# redirects that apply to the loop's combined output. `loopRedirect`
# mirrors `spacedSuffix`'s redirect half — same `redirect` rule, just
# without the arg branch (no positionals after `done`).
loopRedirect     = ws + redirect
loopRedirects    = (loopRedirect)+
forLoop          = forKw + ws + identifier + ws + inKw + loopWords?
                 + sep + doKw + trivias + forBody + trivias? + doneKw
                 + loopRedirects?

# `select NAME in WORDS; do BODY; done` — interactive prompt loop.
# Same grammar shape as `forLoop`; the visitor presents the words as
# a numbered menu via the shell's `promptHandler` and binds NAME to
# the chosen word each iteration. Without a promptHandler configured,
# the loop runs zero iterations (cleanly skips — bash on EOF does the
# same). `break` inside the body exits the loop.
selectLoop       = selectKw + ws + identifier + ws + inKw + loopWords?
                 + sep + doKw + trivias + forBody + trivias? + doneKw
                 + loopRedirects?

# ─── If / elif / else / fi ───────────────────────────────────
# Bash's full conditional. `cond` and `body` are lists of statements;
# the cond's exit status is the **last statement's** success flag, and
# the body runs in textual order. Negative lookaheads on every body
# slot keep the structure keywords from being greedily consumed as
# bareword commands — same trick the for-loop uses for `done`.
ifBlockStmt   = !thenKw + !elifKw + !elseKw + !fiKw + statement
ifBlockStmts  = (ifBlockStmt)+
ifClause      = ifKw + ws + ifBlockStmts + thenKw + trivias? + ifBlockStmts
elifClause    = elifKw + ws + ifBlockStmts + thenKw + trivias? + ifBlockStmts
elifClauses   = (elifClause)+
elseClause    = elseKw + trivias + ifBlockStmts
ifStmt        = ifClause + elifClauses? + elseClause? + fiKw

# ─── While / until loops ────────────────────────────────────
# `while COND; do BODY; done` runs BODY while COND's last statement
# succeeds. `until` is the same with the condition inverted. The body
# reuses the for-loop's `forBody` (its `!doneKw` lookahead is exactly
# what we need); the cond uses a `!doKw` lookahead so it doesn't eat
# `do` as a bareword command.
whileCondStmt  = !doKw + statement
whileCondStmts = (whileCondStmt)+
whileLoop      = whileKw + ws + whileCondStmts + doKw + trivias
               + forBody + trivias? + doneKw + loopRedirects?
untilLoop      = untilKw + ws + whileCondStmts + doKw + trivias
               + forBody + trivias? + doneKw + loopRedirects?

# ─── Case / esac ────────────────────────────────────────────
# `case WORD in PAT) body ;; PAT) body ;& PAT) body ;;& esac`
# Patterns are bash globs (matched via globMatch at runtime). Three
# terminators: `;;` stop, `;&` fall through to the NEXT body
# unconditionally, `;;&` continue testing remaining patterns.
caseTermFall    = ";;&"
caseTermNextEnd = ";&"
caseTermEnd     = ";;"
# Listed longest-first so the matcher commits to the longer literal.
caseTerminator  = caseTermFall | caseTermEnd | caseTermNextEnd

casePatternAlt  = ws? + "|" + ws? + word
casePatternAlts = (casePatternAlt)+
casePattern     = word + casePatternAlts?

caseBodyStmt    = !caseTerminator + !esacKw + statement
caseBody        = (caseBodyStmt)+

caseClause      = casePattern + ws? + ")" + trivias?
                + caseBody? + ws? + caseTerminator
# Named the repeat element so each clause is a direct, predictable child
# of `caseClauses` — `(trivias? + caseClause)+` would create an anonymous
# wrapper pattern.
caseClauseEntry = trivias? + caseClause
caseClauses     = (caseClauseEntry)+

caseStmt        = caseKw + ws + word + ws + inKw + trivias
                + caseClauses? + trivias? + esacKw

# ─── Functions ──────────────────────────────────────────────
# Two declaration forms — POSIX `name() body` and bash's
# `function name [()] body`. Body is a `{ … }` group; the closing
# `}` is kept out of the body via a `!closeBrace` lookahead so
# `(funcBodyStmt)+` doesn't greedily consume it as a bareword.
closeBrace    = "}"
funcBodyStmt  = !closeBrace + statement
# Pulling the repeat into its own named rule (rather than inline inside
# `funcBody`) gives cleaner AST children — no anonymous-pattern wrapper.
funcBodyStmts = (funcBodyStmt)+
funcBody      = "{" + ws + trivias? + funcBodyStmts + trivias? + closeBrace
# `trivias?` (OPTIONAL), not `trivias`: bash accepts `f(){ …; }` with no
# space between `)` and `{`, and it is a common style. The body itself still
# requires `"{" + ws`, which is what keeps a brace GROUP distinguishable from
# a brace EXPANSION, so nothing is made ambiguous by relaxing this.
funcDefPosix  = identifier + ws? + "(" + ws? + ")" + trivias? + funcBody
funcDefBash   = functionKw + ws + identifier + (ws? + "(" + ws? + ")")? + trivias? + funcBody
funcDef       = funcDefBash | funcDefPosix

# ─── Brace group — `{ list; }` ──────────────────────────────
# POSIX compound command: runs `list` in the CURRENT shell (unlike a
# `(subshell)`, which copies the frame — so assignments persist and
# exit/return/break/continue propagate). Disambiguated from brace
# EXPANSION (`{a,b}`) by the REQUIRED whitespace after `{` (expansion has
# none) — same `"{" + ws` shape funcBody uses. Reuses `funcBodyStmts`
# (`(!closeBrace + statement)+`). `loopRedirects?` allows `{ …; } > out`.
braceGroup    = "{" + ws + trivias? + funcBodyStmts + trivias? + closeBrace + loopRedirects?

# ─── return / local / shift ─────────────────────────────────
returnArg  = ws + word
returnStmt = returnKw + returnArg?
# `local NAME[=VALUE] …` — multiple bindings allowed per call.
# Each binding parses as an `assignment` (so `=value` is required when
# the form has a value); a bare `local x` just declares without setting,
# which we treat as setting to empty.
localBinding   = ws + assignment
localBareName  = ws + identifier
localItem      = localBinding | localBareName
localItems     = (localItem)+
localStmt      = localKw + localItems

# `export [-n|-p] NAME[=value]…` — mark names for the ENVIRONMENT, i.e. the
# variables a child BODY inherits (a `$PATH` dynamic tool, a script tool). Bash
# passes a child process only the exported set; assignment alone is shell-local.
# `-n` unexports, `-p`/bare `export` lists. Same item shape as `local` so
# `export A=1 B` parses in one statement.
exportBinding  = ws + assignment
exportBareWord = ws + word
exportItem     = exportBinding | exportBareWord
exportItems    = (exportItem)+
exportStmt     = exportKw + exportItems?

# ─── unset / readonly / eval / let / type / command ─────────
# Six builtins that had no implementation anywhere. `unset` is the notable
# absence: `set -u` was fully supported while the builtin that makes nounset
# usable was missing, and a script that called it died with exit 127.
#
# All are grammar-level statements rather than registered tools because each
# needs the FRAME — to delete a variable, re-enter the parser in the current
# scope, assign an arithmetic result, or resolve a shell function by name. A
# tool only ever sees its argv.

# Each arg slot carries a `!redirect` lookahead so the greedy repetition stops
# at a redirect instead of swallowing it — without it the `2` of
# `unset v 2>/dev/null` is read as an argument and the `>` has nowhere to go.
# The generic `command` rule solves the same problem the other way round, by
# trying `redirect` before `arg` in every suffix slot.
#
# Each takes a NAMED wrapper around its `(arg)+` repetition — an inline
# repetition produces an anonymous node, and the visitor's arg reader would
# find no children to walk.
#
# All six also carry `loopRedirects?`, reusing the machinery `{ …; } > out`
# and `done < file` already use. Without it `type foo >/dev/null 2>&1` — the
# single most common way either probe is written — is a PARSE ERROR, since a
# grammar-level statement is not a `command` and the redirect has nowhere to
# attach.

# `unset [-v|-f] NAME…` — remove variables, array elements (`unset 'a[1]'`)
# or functions. Bareword args so `unset 'a[1]'` and `unset $name` both work.
unsetArg   = ws + !redirect + word
unsetArgs  = (unsetArg)+
unsetStmt  = unsetKw + unsetArgs + loopRedirects?

# `readonly [-p] [NAME[=VALUE]]…` — same item shape as `export`, since both
# mark names and both accept an inline assignment.
readonlyStmt = readonlyKw + exportItems? + loopRedirects?

# `eval ARG…` — concatenate the arguments with spaces and run the result as
# shell input, in the CURRENT frame.
evalArg    = ws + !redirect + word
evalArgs   = (evalArg)+
evalStmt   = evalKw + evalArgs? + loopRedirects?

# `let EXPR…` — evaluate each argument as an arithmetic expression. Exit
# status is 0 when the LAST expression is non-zero, mirroring `((…))`.
letArg     = ws + !redirect + word
letArgs    = (letArg)+
letStmt    = letKw + letArgs + loopRedirects?

# `type [-t|-p|-a] NAME…` and `command [-v|-V] NAME [ARG…]`.
typeArg    = ws + !redirect + word
typeArgs   = (typeArg)+
typeStmt   = typeKw + typeArgs + loopRedirects?
commandArg = ws + !redirect + word
commandArgs = (commandArg)+
commandStmt = commandKw + commandArgs + loopRedirects?
shiftArg       = ws + word
shiftStmt      = shiftKw + shiftArg?
# `trap ACTION SIGNAL…` — register ACTION (a command string) to run on a
# signal. Requires the action + at least one signal name. The single
# meaningful signal here is `EXIT` (fires when the top-level script ends);
# others are stored but inert in this single-process shell.
trapArg        = ws + word
trapArgs       = (trapArg)+
trapStmt       = trapKw + trapArgs

# `alias [name[=value] …]` / `unalias [-a] name…`. Each arg is one word —
# `name='ls -la'` arrives as a single word (the quotes concatenate), and
# the visitor splits it on the first `=`. Bare `alias` (no args) prints the
# table; `unalias` requires at least one arg (a name or `-a`).
aliasArg       = ws + word
aliasArgs      = (aliasArg)+
aliasStmt      = aliasKw + aliasArgs?
unaliasStmt    = unaliasKw + aliasArgs

# `. FILE [args…]` and `source FILE [args…]`. The file path is the first
# arg; any additional args become the file's positional params ($1..$N)
# during execution. The keyword regex (above) keeps `.` from absorbing
# bareword chars in `./script.sh`, so the file path still parses as a
# normal word containing slashes/dots.
sourceArg      = ws + word
sourceArgs     = (sourceArg)+
sourceKw       = sourceLongKw | sourceShortKw
# Args are optional in the grammar so `source` with no args parses and
# the visitor can emit the bash-style "filename argument required"
# diagnostic. Without `?`, the rule fails and `source` falls through
# to a generic command, producing a less helpful "Command not found".
sourceStmt     = sourceKw + sourceArgs?

# `read [-r] [VAR…]` — read one line from stdin and assign it to VARs
# (splitting on $IFS). With no VAR names, the line lands in `REPLY`.
# With multiple VARs, the last one collects the remainder of the line
# (trailing fields plus their IFS separators). Implemented as a
# grammar-level statement (not a tool) because it needs to mutate the
# caller's `frame.vars` and consume from `frame.stdin`.
#
# Each suffix is either a redirect (`read x < file`, `read x <<< "$y"`)
# or a word (flag like `-r` or a var name). The visitor classifies
# words after evaluation. Mirrors how `command` is built (commandSuffix
# = redirect | arg), but uses `word` directly because `read` doesn't
# accept `--key=value` named-arg syntax.
readKw           = /read(?![a-zA-Z0-9_-])/
readSuffix       = redirect | word
readSpacedSuffix = ws? + readSuffix
# Name the repeat (not `(readSpacedSuffix)*` inline) so the AST has a
# predictable `readSuffixes` child rather than an anonymous wrapper —
# same gotcha as `caseClauses`, `whileCondStmts`, `funcBodyStmts`.
readSuffixes     = (readSpacedSuffix)+
readStmt         = readKw + readSuffixes?

# `mapfile [-t] [-d DELIM] [-n N] [-s S] arr` (also `readarray`, an
# exact alias). Reads all of stdin into the indexed array `arr`, one
# element per line. With `-t`, trailing newlines are stripped from
# each line. Same suffix shape as `read`; the visitor parses flags
# and the final var name from the args.
mapfileKw        = /mapfile(?![a-zA-Z0-9_-])/
readarrayKw      = /readarray(?![a-zA-Z0-9_-])/
mapfileNameKw    = mapfileKw | readarrayKw
mapfileSuffix    = redirect | word
mapfileSpacedSuffix = ws? + mapfileSuffix
mapfileSuffixes  = (mapfileSpacedSuffix)+
mapfileStmt      = mapfileNameKw + mapfileSuffixes?

# `set [-eEunxv]…` / `set -o NAME` / `set -- args…` — shell option
# toggles and positional-parameter replacement. Same suffix shape as
# `read`: each arg is a word (flag like `-e`, `+u`, the literal `-o`,
# or a positional value). Repeat is named to avoid the inline-anon
# wrapper trap.
setKw           = /set(?![a-zA-Z0-9_-])/
setArg          = ws + word
setArgs         = (setArg)+
setStmt         = setKw + setArgs?

# `declare [-a|-A|-aA|…] name[=value]…` — declare a variable or array
# with optional attributes. The most common forms are `declare -a arr`
# (indexed array) and `declare -A m` (associative array — REQUIRED
# because without it, `m[key]=v` would treat the subscript as
# arithmetic and assign to `arr[0]`). Same suffix shape as `set`.
declareKw       = /declare(?![a-zA-Z0-9_-])/
# A declare item is either an array initializer (`arr=(a b c)` — tried
# first so its `=(…)` isn't mis-tokenized as separate words) or a plain
# word (a `-flag`, a bare NAME, or a scalar `NAME=value`). This is what
# makes the combined `declare -a arr=(a b c)` one-liner parse.
declareItem     = arrayInit | word
declareArg      = ws + declareItem
declareArgs     = (declareArg)+
declareStmt     = declareKw + declareArgs?

# `shopt [-s|-u] [NAME…]` — toggle shell-behavior options. Subset:
# `extglob`, `nullglob`, `dotglob`, etc. `-s NAME` enables, `-u NAME`
# disables. Bare `shopt` (no args) lists all (we just return success).
shoptKw         = /shopt(?![a-zA-Z0-9_-])/
shoptArg        = ws + word
shoptArgs       = (shoptArg)+
shoptStmt       = shoptKw + shoptArgs?

# `getopts OPTSTRING VARNAME [ARGS]` — parse one positional option per
# call. Reads/writes shell-managed vars (OPTIND, OPTARG, the named
# var), so it's a grammar-level statement (visitor needs frame access).
# Returns success while options remain; failure when args are exhausted
# or a non-option arg is reached. Common idiom:
#   while getopts "vf:" opt; do case $opt in v) verbose=1;; f) file=$OPTARG;; esac; done
getoptsKw       = /getopts(?![a-zA-Z0-9_-])/
getoptsArg      = ws + word
getoptsArgs     = (getoptsArg)+
getoptsStmt     = getoptsKw + getoptsArgs?

# ─── [[ ]] compound conditional ─────────────────────────────
# Bash's enhanced test. Differences from `test`/`[`:
#   - && / || / ! are logical operators within the form (not pipe
#     operators), with proper precedence (! highest, then &&, then ||)
#   - == / != do glob matching; =~ matches regex; <, > do lexicographic
#     string compare (with `[ ]` they'd be redirection)
#   - No word splitting on unquoted expansions inside the form
dbOpenKw    = "[["
dbCloseKw   = "]]"

# Operators. Inside `dbBinaryOp` the longer literals come first so the
# matcher commits to `==` before `=`, `<=` before `<`, etc.
dbUnaryOp   = "-z" | "-n" | "-e" | "-f" | "-d" | "-s" | "-v"
            | "-r" | "-w" | "-x"
dbBinaryOp  = "==" | "!=" | "=~" | "<=" | ">="
            | "-eq" | "-ne" | "-lt" | "-le" | "-gt" | "-ge"
            | "=" | "<" | ">"

# ─── The `=~` regex operand ─────────────────────────────────
# The right side of `=~` is a REGEX, not a glob or a filename, so it routinely
# contains `(`, `|`, `{`, `^`, `+` — characters `bareword` deliberately
# excludes because everywhere else they are shell syntax. With only `word`
# available, `[[ abc =~ (a)(b) ]]` was a PARSE ERROR that killed the whole
# script, which ruled out capture groups: the main reason to reach for `=~`.
#
# `regexBareword` takes any run of non-space characters, plus a `]` that is
# NOT the start of the closing `]]` — so a character class (`[a-c]`) survives
# while the terminator still ends the operand. Expansions and quoted strings
# are tried first, so `[[ $x =~ $re ]]` and `[[ $x =~ "lit" ]]` still work.
regexBareword = /(?:\\.|\](?!\])|[^\s\]])+/
regexWord     = (expansion | sqString | dqString | regexBareword)+
dbRegexOp     = "=~"

# Atoms (non-self-recursive) — listed inside `dbExpr` below.
dbAtomRegex  = word + ws + dbRegexOp + ws + regexWord
dbAtomBinary = word + ws + dbBinaryOp + ws + word
dbAtomUnary  = dbUnaryOp + ws + word
dbAtomParen  = "(" + ws? + dbExpr + ws? + ")"
dbAtomSingle = word

# Logic operators. cpat auto-classifies a rule by where the self-ref
# (dbExpr) appears: at end → prefix, at start AND end → infix.
dbAndOp = "&&"
dbOrOp  = "||"
dbNotOp = "!"

dbNot   = dbNotOp + ws + dbExpr
dbAnd   = dbExpr + ws + dbAndOp + ws + dbExpr
dbOr    = dbExpr + ws + dbOrOp  + ws + dbExpr

# Order matters: declare higher-precedence operators first (! > && > ||),
# and ensure atoms come AFTER the operator/atom-binary rules so a single
# bareword doesn't shortcut a binary form like `word OP word`.
# `dbAtomRegex` precedes `dbAtomBinary` so the permissive regex operand wins
# over `dbBinaryOp`'s plain-`word` right side whenever the operator is `=~`.
dbExpr  = dbNot | dbAnd | dbOr
        | dbAtomRegex | dbAtomBinary | dbAtomUnary | dbAtomParen | dbAtomSingle

dblBracketStmt = dbOpenKw + ws + dbExpr + ws + dbCloseKw

# ─── Break / continue / exit ────────────────────────────────
# Loop control. Outside a loop, the visitor surfaces break/continue as
# `success: false` with an explanatory stderr (matching bash). `exit`
# halts the enclosing script — or the subshell, if inside one — via a
# signal sentinel caught at the appropriate boundary.
# The optional count is bash's "break out of N enclosing loops". Without it
# `break 2` failed to parse the ENCLOSING loop, not just the statement, so a
# nested-loop script died with `Command not found: for`.
loopLevel    = ws + word
breakStmt    = breakKw + loopLevel?
continueStmt = continueKw + loopLevel?
exitArg      = ws + word
exitStmt     = exitKw + exitArg?

# ─── Arithmetic expressions ─────────────────────────────────
# Shared sub-grammar for the three arithmetic call sites:
#   `$((expr))`     — arithExpansion, slots into `expansion`
#   `((expr))`      — arithCommand,   slots into `expr` and `negatable`
#   `for ((;;));…`  — arithFor,       slots into `expr` and `negatable`
#
# All three use the same `arithExpr` Expression pattern. cpat
# auto-classifies each alternative by structure (atom / prefix /
# postfix / infix). Declaration order determines precedence —
# **earliest = highest precedence (binds tighter)**. The `right`
# keyword on `arithPower`, `arithTernary`, and `arithAssign` gives
# them right-associativity to match bash.
#
# Multi-char operators must be listed before any single-char prefix
# in their Options (`**` before `*`, `==` before `=`, `<<=` before
# `<<` before `<=` before `<`, `&&` before `&`, `||` before `|`).

# Integer literals: an explicit base (`2#101`, `16#ff`), hex (`0xFF`),
# octal (`0` followed by 0-7 digits, matching bash's leading-zero rule),
# or decimal (`0` alone, or any non-leading-zero number).
#
# `BASE#DIGITS` comes FIRST so `2#101` is not read as the number 2 followed
# by a stray `#`. Bash allows bases 2-64 with digits 0-9 a-z A-Z @ _; the
# range check is the evaluator's job, so the pattern stays permissive.
arithInt        = /[0-9]+#[0-9a-zA-Z@_]+|0[xX][0-9a-fA-F]+|0[0-7]+|[1-9][0-9]*|0/

# Atom: variable read via bare identifier (`i`) or `$VAR` / `${VAR}`,
# plus special positionals via `$1`..`$9` / `$#` / `$@` / `$*` / `$?`.
arithVar        = identifier
arithDollarRef  = "$" + identifier
arithDollarBrc  = "${" + identifier + "}"
arithDollarSpec = "$" + specialVarName
arithParen      = "(" + ws? + arithExpr + ws? + ")"

# Operator literals. Where a shorter operator is a prefix of a
# longer one (`&` ⊂ `&&`, `|` ⊂ `||`, `<` ⊂ `<=` / `<<`, `=` ⊂ `==`,
# `*` ⊂ `**` / `*=`, etc.), the shorter one uses a **negative-
# lookahead regex** so cpat's PEG parser doesn't greedily consume
# the first character and then fail to backtrack into the longer
# operator. Without this, `1 && 2` would parse `&` as bitwise-and,
# fail to find a RHS, and never reach arithLogAnd.
#
# Compound assignments (`+=`, `*=`, `<<=`, etc.) are listed first
# in their Options so `i = j == 5` parses as `i = (j == 5)` —
# `=` (assign) wouldn't conflict here, but the same length-first
# pattern keeps things readable.
arithPostfixOp  = "++" | "--"
# Prefix `+` / `-` / `!` must not eat the first char of `+=` /
# `-=` / `!=`. But prefix is only ever tried at the start of an
# arithExpr (atom-scan phase), so the only risk is if a unary
# prefix appears immediately before a compound-assign'd identifier —
# extremely unlikely in practice. We still guard `!` from `!=`
# because `!=` is also a valid operator slot and the ambiguity is
# real if a `!` shows up where an infix op could.
arithPrefixOp   = "++" | "--" | "+" | "-" | /!(?!=)/ | "~"
arithPowerOp    = "**"
arithMulDivOp   = /\*(?![*=])/ | /\/(?!=)/ | /%(?!=)/
arithAddSubOp   = /\+(?!=)/ | /-(?!=)/
arithShiftOp    = /<<(?!=)/ | />>(?!=)/
arithCompareOp  = "<=" | ">=" | /<(?![<=])/ | />(?![>=])/
arithEqualityOp = "==" | "!="
arithBitAndOp   = /&(?![&=])/
arithBitXorOp   = /\^(?!=)/
arithBitOrOp    = /\|(?![|=])/
arithLogAndOp   = "&&"
arithLogOrOp    = "||"
arithAssignOp   = "**=" | "<<=" | ">>=" | "+=" | "-=" | "*=" | "/=" | "%="
                | "&=" | "|=" | "^=" | /=(?!=)/
arithCommaOp    = ","

# Self-referencing rules — cpat auto-classifies these into prefix /
# postfix / infix based on where the self-ref appears. arithParen
# is an atom despite containing arithExpr because the self-ref is
# wrapped in literal `(` / `)` (neither boundary is the self-ref).
arithPostfix    = arithExpr + ws? + arithPostfixOp
arithPrefix     = arithPrefixOp + ws? + arithExpr
arithPower      = arithExpr + ws? + arithPowerOp    + ws? + arithExpr
arithMulDiv     = arithExpr + ws? + arithMulDivOp   + ws? + arithExpr
arithAddSub     = arithExpr + ws? + arithAddSubOp   + ws? + arithExpr
arithShift      = arithExpr + ws? + arithShiftOp    + ws? + arithExpr
arithCompare    = arithExpr + ws? + arithCompareOp  + ws? + arithExpr
arithEquality   = arithExpr + ws? + arithEqualityOp + ws? + arithExpr
arithBitAnd     = arithExpr + ws? + arithBitAndOp   + ws? + arithExpr
arithBitXor     = arithExpr + ws? + arithBitXorOp   + ws? + arithExpr
arithBitOr      = arithExpr + ws? + arithBitOrOp    + ws? + arithExpr
arithLogAnd     = arithExpr + ws? + arithLogAndOp   + ws? + arithExpr
arithLogOr      = arithExpr + ws? + arithLogOrOp    + ws? + arithExpr
arithTernary    = arithExpr + ws? + "?" + ws? + arithExpr + ws? + ":" + ws? + arithExpr
arithAssign     = arithExpr + ws? + arithAssignOp   + ws? + arithExpr
arithComma      = arithExpr + ws? + arithCommaOp    + ws? + arithExpr

# Expression: ordered by precedence (highest first). `right`
# keyword marks right-associative infix operators. Atoms last so
# operators match before raw literals (Expression Pattern picks
# atoms during initial scan regardless of position, but we keep
# them at the bottom of the list for clarity).
arithExpr = arithPostfix | arithPrefix | arithPower right | arithMulDiv
          | arithAddSub | arithShift | arithCompare | arithEquality
          | arithBitAnd | arithBitXor | arithBitOr | arithLogAnd
          | arithLogOr | arithTernary right | arithAssign right
          | arithComma
          | arithParen | arithDollarBrc | arithDollarSpec | arithDollarRef
          | arithInt | arithVar

# ─── Arithmetic command + arithmetic for-loop ───────────────
# `(( expr ))` is a standalone arithmetic command. Bash's exit
# semantics for this construct are **inverted** from normal
# commands: success when the result is non-zero, failure when
# zero. The visitor implements that — it lets `((i > 0)) && …`
# read naturally.
# `((` at command position COMMITS to the arithmetic command (the `~/`),
# mirroring the `$((` cut above: `((echo hi))`-style input is an arith
# syntax error, and nested subshells are written `( (…) )` with a space —
# the POSIX-recommended spelling. Without the cut, `(((((…` cross-
# backtracked between this rule and `subshell` at every depth (6+ seconds
# at 100 parens, growing without bound).
arithCommand = "((" ~/ ws? + arithExpr + ws? + "))"

# `for ((init; cond; update)); do BODY; done`. Each slot is
# optional (`for ((;;))` is the canonical infinite loop, capped
# by Shell.maxLoopIterations). Body, terminator, and trailing
# redirects come from the list-form for-loop machinery above.
arithForHead = forKw + ws + "((" + ws? + arithExpr? + ws? + ";"
             + ws? + arithExpr? + ws? + ";"
             + ws? + arithExpr? + ws? + "))"
arithFor     = arithForHead + sep + doKw + trivias + forBody
             + trivias? + doneKw + loopRedirects?

# ─── Negation (!) ───────────────────────────────────────────
# `! expr` flips the success bit while preserving stdout/stderr.
# Binds to a single primary, not to a binaryExpr — so
# `! a && b` parses as `(!a) && b`. To negate a whole pipeline,
# wrap it in a subshell: `! (a | b)`.
# `arithFor` and `arithCommand` are listed before `forLoop` /
# `subshell` so their `((` prefix wins first-match over single
# `(`. `forLoop` still has to come before plain `command` for the
# same keyword-vs-bareword reason as before.
negatable   = arithFor | arithCommand | forLoop | prefixedCommand
            | assignment | subshell | braceGroup | command
notOp       = "!"
negatedExpr = notOp + ws + negatable

# ─── Binary operators (Expression-promoted infix) ───────────
# Operator tokens. Listed longest-first so the matcher commits to
# the longer literal (e.g. `||` before `|`).
andOp      = "&&"
orOp       = "||"
# Negative lookahead so `|` doesn't greedily match the first half of
# `||`. Same tokenization trick used by `arithBitOrOp` above. Without
# this, `cmd1 || cmd2` would parse the first `|` as a `pipeOp`, then
# fail to find a second `expr` because the remaining `| cmd2` is a
# stray `|`. (When the operators all lived in one `binaryOp` flat
# alternation, the alternation order — `orOp | andOp | pipeOp` — was
# sufficient because longer literals were tried first. With each
# operator promoted to its own precedence-level rule, the longest-first
# guarantee is lost; tokenization disambiguation now lives in the regex
# itself.)
pipeOp     = /\|(?!\|)/
# One rule per precedence level, each defined as `expr + op + expr`
# (full recursion on both sides). cpat's Expression Pattern uses
# the alternation order in `expr` (below) to encode precedence —
# tightest binding listed first. Bash precedence:
#   `|`  > `&&` > `||`
# so `a && b | c` parses as `a && (b | c)`, and
#    `a || b && c` parses as `a || (b && c)`.
# Same shape as the arithmetic operators (arithMulDiv / arithAddSub /
# arithLogAnd / arithLogOr above) — they all share the Expression
# Pattern convention.
#
# Right-side trivia (after the operator) is `trivias?` rather than
# `ws?` so a newline IMMEDIATELY after `&&` / `||` / `|` is treated
# as implicit line continuation — the operator demands a right
# operand, so the newline can't terminate the statement there. Matches
# bash. Left-side stays `ws?`: a newline BEFORE the operator
# terminates the previous statement (also matches bash — `cmd\n&& x`
# is a syntax error in real bash).
pipeExpr   = expr + ws? + pipeOp + trivias? + expr
andExpr    = expr + ws? + andOp  + trivias? + expr
orExpr     = expr + ws? + orOp   + trivias? + expr
# Loop atoms (forLoop, breakStmt, continueStmt) and the script-control
# atom (exitStmt) are listed before `command` so their word-bounded
# keyword regexes win first-match over the generic `bareword`.
# arithFor / arithCommand come ahead of forLoop / subshell so their
# `((` prefix beats single `(`.
# Binary operators come FIRST and IN PRECEDENCE ORDER (highest binding
# first): pipeExpr > andExpr > orExpr. Atoms (command, subshell, …)
# go at the tail.
expr       = pipeExpr | andExpr | orExpr
           | negatedExpr | arithFor | arithCommand
           | forLoop | selectLoop | whileLoop | untilLoop | ifStmt | caseStmt
           | funcDef | dblBracketStmt
           | breakStmt | continueStmt | exitStmt
           | builtinStmt
           | arrayInit | arrayIndexedAssign
           | prefixedBuiltin | prefixedCommand | assignment | subshell | braceGroup | command

# The grammar-level builtins, named as a group so the prefix form below can
# reference them without restating the list.
builtinStmt = returnStmt | localStmt | exportStmt | shiftStmt | trapStmt | sourceStmt | readStmt | setStmt
            | aliasStmt | unaliasStmt | mapfileStmt | declareStmt | shoptStmt | getoptsStmt
            | unsetStmt | readonlyStmt | evalStmt | letStmt | typeStmt | commandStmt

# `VAR=value builtin …` — a variable prefix in front of a grammar-level
# builtin. `IFS=: read -r a b` is the canonical case and it did not parse at
# all: `prefixedCommand` only accepts a `command`, so `IFS=: read` fell
# through to the generic command path, looked for a TOOL named `read`, and
# died with `Command not found: read` — while the very same script with
# `IFS=:` on its own line worked. Listed before `prefixedCommand` so the
# builtin wins over the tool lookup.
prefixedBuiltin = prefixList + builtinStmt

# ─── Top level ──────────────────────────────────────────────
# A `;` only counts as a statement separator when it's not the start of a
# case-terminator (`;;`, `;&`, `;;&`). Otherwise the regular statement
# parser would greedily eat the terminator and leave the case clause
# unparseable. Newlines have no such collision.
sepCore       = /(?:;(?![;&])|\n)+/
sep           = ws? + comment? + sepCore + trivias?
statement     = expr + sep?
statementList = (statement)+
script        = trivias? + statementList + trivias?
